junction.name: Atlantic Avenue & Utica Avenue, New York City

claims.text: Atlantic Avenue & Utica Avenue had 87 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 14 pedestrians injured, 7 cyclists injured and 0 people killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $6.0 million a year.
40% of crashes here had “driver inattention/distraction” recorded as a contributing factor, against 27% at the city's priority junctions.
37% of crashes here had only people in vehicles hurt, against 24% at the city's priority junctions.
Held up on later years: only people in vehicles hurt in 40% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 24% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search).

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: passed the causal gate (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).
Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 2.6 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: the record FHWA cites), worth $894,000 a year.

Yellow Change Intervals would avoid about 1.4 crashes a year (CMF 4219, the more conservative of the two middle records of 4; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $465,000 a year; check on site: the current yellow plus all-red time is below the ITE recommended practice.
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for Atlantic Avenue, Utica Avenue (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 36, New York City Council; Brooklyn Community Board 8.
A request letter to the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is drafted and checked.

draft_request.letter:
To: the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
Cc: Council Member, District 36, New York City Council; Brooklyn Community Board 8
Subject: Subject: Request for safety studies and signal timing review — Atlantic Avenue & Utica Avenue

Dear colleagues at NYC DOT,

We are writing to ask your agency to conduct safety studies and consider low-cost fixes at the junction of Atlantic Avenue & Utica Avenue, on the roads it is responsible for.

Our review of the official city records for the 5 years from 31 October 2021 shows 180 crashes, including 87 crashes that caused injury. Among those hurt were 14 pedestrians and 7 cyclists. No one was killed. The harm valued at $6.0 million per year in the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars). Our check found no safety project recorded at this junction in this period. This location is listed with city priority location status, which adds to our concern.

We ask you to review the recent crash history and site conditions at this junction and, where conditions allow, consider the following fixes on your roads:

* longer yellow signal times (federally as Yellow Change Intervals). This fix is expected to prevent about 4.7 injury crashes per year. This would avoid about $1,621,000 in harm per year. Costs should be checked on site, but federal estimates suggest it pays for itself under $11.4 million.
* reflective backplates on the traffic signals (federally as Backplates with Retroreflective Borders). This fix is expected to prevent about 2.6 injury crashes per year. This would avoid about $894,000 in harm per year. Costs should be checked on site, but federal estimates suggest it pays for itself under $6.3 million.

Where the city installed a leading pedestrian interval (a walk signal a few seconds before the green) at 1,651 intersections, pedestrian injury crashes fell 17 percent (95 percent interval 11 percent to 22 percent) compared with intersections that got it later; a stricter check against fake programs is less certain. We ask you to consider this where there is a turning movement, after a site check.

Please let us know the outcome of your study and what steps you plan to take.

Yours sincerely,

[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]

Sources:
- NYC Open Data, Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95)
- NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (corridors); NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (intersections); NYC Vision Zero View, Enhanced Crossings (6ax4-q5k4); NYC Vision Zero View, Leading Pedestrian Interval Signals; NYC Vision Zero View, Signal Timing/25 MPH Retiming; NYC Vision Zero View, Speed Humps (jknp-skuy); NYC Vision Zero View, Turn Traffic Calming; NYC Vision Zero priority corridors; NYC Vision Zero priority intersections
- FHWA CMF Clearinghouse, CMF 4215 (longer yellow signal times)
- FHWA CMF Clearinghouse, CMF 1410 (reflective backplates on the traffic signals)
- U.S. DOT Benefit-Cost Analysis Guidance, 2026 Update, Table A-1 (2024 dollars)
- NearMissLens NML-Bench T11: before/after study of the city's own installs (validation/BENCH.md)
- Road owners: the registry's road-inventory layer (see the engineer report's receipts)
